title: Beer
summary: Beer is water carrying sugars, alcohol, bitterness, aroma, yeast character, colour, gas and foam. A brewer makes those parts by mashing malt, boiling wort with hops, fermenting, conditioning and packaging. Temperature, time, pitch rate, pH and gas pressure move the result, while measurements tell you when the process is ready. Styles and vessels are surfaces that can change without changing the underlying brewing system.

nodes.plain: The beer as a drinker meets it: liquid in a vessel, with aroma, colour, carbonation and a head.
nodes.ask: Does this pint deliver the intended balance, freshness and drinking experience?

nodes.plain: Water is the main liquid in beer. Its minerals and alkalinity shape mash pH, flavour and mouthfeel.
nodes.does: Carries dissolved extract and sets the chemical starting point for the mash.
nodes.ask: What water profile and alkalinity will let this grist reach its target pH?

sources.label: Martin Brungard, Bru'n Water: Water Knowledge
sources.flag: opened in this run

nodes.does: Changes mash chemistry and flavour by supplying ions and buffering acidity.
nodes.plain: Calcium, magnesium, sulphate, chloride, sodium and bicarbonate change mash chemistry and the way beer tastes.
nodes.ask: Which ions are present, and what alkalinity will they leave after the malt reacts?

feel.why: Small ions quietly steer the mash and the final flavour.

sources.label: Martin Brungard, Bru'n Water: Water Knowledge

nodes.plain: The brewer chooses whether to use source water, reverse-osmosis water, or treated water with salts and acid.
nodes.does: Moves alkalinity and mineral concentrations towards the style and mash target.
nodes.ask: Do I need to dilute, add minerals or add acid for this grist?
nodes.range: Source water; RO or distilled water; mineral salts; acid additions

items.name: Source water with report
items.plain: Use the measured water report and adjust only what the grist needs.

sources.label: Martin Brungard, Bru'n Water: Water Knowledge

items.name: RO water plus salts
items.plain: Start with low-alkalinity water and rebuild calcium, sulphate and chloride deliberately.

sources.label: Martin Brungard, Bru'n Water: Water Knowledge

items.name: Distilled water plus salts
items.plain: Use a blank water base, then add a measured mineral profile.

sources.label: Martin Brungard, Bru'n Water: Water Knowledge

nodes.plain: Malt supplies fermentable sugars plus larger dextrins, proteins and minerals that remain to give beer body.
nodes.does: Feeds fermentation and sets sweetness, dryness, texture and foam potential.
nodes.ask: How much sugar should ferment, and how much body should remain?

sources.label: Brewers Association, Hop Creep Technical Brief
sources.flag: wort extract composition

nodes.plain: These dissolved sugars are food for yeast. Maltose is the principal fermentable sugar in wort.
nodes.does: Supplies the carbon and energy that become alcohol, carbon dioxide and new yeast.
nodes.ask: Is the wort fermentable enough for the intended final gravity?

sources.label: Brewers Association, Hop Creep Technical Brief

nodes.plain: Longer-chain sugars survive fermentation and add fullness, sweetness and viscosity.
nodes.does: Keeps the beer from feeling thin and gives malt and foam a scaffold.
nodes.ask: How much residual extract should this beer carry?

sources.label: Brewers Association, Hop Creep Technical Brief

nodes.plain: Yeast turns fermentable sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Ethanol gives warmth and changes body and preservation.
nodes.does: Sets strength, warmth and part of the balance against sweetness and bitterness.
nodes.ask: Is the alcohol level right for the style and drinkability?

sources.label: Brewers Association, Hop Creep Technical Brief

nodes.does: Provides warmth and changes the balance between sweetness, body and bitterness.
nodes.plain: Ethanol is the principal alcohol made when yeast ferments wort sugars.
nodes.ask: How much ethanol should this fermentation produce?

feel.why: Alcohol feels warm and light but can become sharp when it is too high.

sources.label: Brewers Association, Hop Creep Technical Brief

nodes.plain: ABV estimates the percentage of the finished beer that is ethanol, commonly from the change between OG and FG.
nodes.does: Compares strength with the recipe and style target.
nodes.ask: What ABV did the measured OG and FG produce?
nodes.range: About 0–20% ABV for ordinary beers; calculate from OG and FG

nodes.plain: Boiled hop alpha acids become bitter compounds that balance malt sweetness.
nodes.does: Provides the bitter counterweight that keeps beer from tasting cloying.
nodes.ask: How much bitterness should the beer carry, and how clean should it feel?

sources.label: Grainfather, Calculation – IBU

nodes.does: Carries hop bitterness into wort after heat converts the acids.
nodes.plain: Heat transforms hop alpha acids into more soluble iso-alpha acids during the boil.
nodes.ask: What hop charge, gravity and time will give the intended bitterness?

feel.why: Heat folds a plant molecule into a sharper, more forceful bitter edge.

sources.label: Brad Smith, Recipe Formulation and Ingredients

nodes.plain: IBU is a laboratory or modelled measure of bittering material, usually expressed as milligrams per litre of iso-alpha acids.
nodes.does: Sets a repeatable bitterness target while reminding the brewer that perception is not only a number.
nodes.ask: What IBU should this recipe target, and how will the model handle late hops?
nodes.range: Often about 5–100 IBU; recipe estimates depend on gravity, time, hop form and temperature

nodes.plain: Volatile hop oils and compounds give floral, herbal, citrus, resinous or tropical aromas.
nodes.does: Signals the hop variety and timing before the first sip.
nodes.ask: Which hop compounds should reach the glass without being boiled away or oxidised?

sources.label: Brad Smith, Recipe Formulation and Ingredients

nodes.does: Carries volatile hop character into the beer and fades when heat or oxygen strips it.
nodes.plain: Hop oils are volatile compounds that carry much of a hop's aroma; late and dry-hop additions preserve more of them.
nodes.ask: Which variety and contact time gives the aroma without grassy or oxidised notes?

feel.why: Aroma compounds feel light, fast and easily lost to heat or oxygen.

sources.label: Brad Smith, Recipe Formulation and Ingredients

nodes.plain: Yeast leaves compounds such as esters, phenols, sulphur notes and a clean or expressive fermentation profile.
nodes.does: Adds character and finishes the conversion of wort into beer.

nodes.plain: Yeast metabolism creates flavour compounds as well as alcohol and carbon dioxide.

nodes.plain: Malt colour and boiling history make the beer look pale, amber, brown or black.
nodes.does: Sets the first visual cue and often travels with roast, toast and caramel flavour.

nodes.does: Provides the coloured malt compounds that set the beer's visual range.
nodes.plain: Pale, kilned, crystal and roasted malts contribute different colour and flavour compounds.

feel.why: Roasting makes colour feel heavier, warmer and more granular.

nodes.plain: SRM is the common colour scale in the United States; EBC is roughly twice the SRM value.
nodes.does: Turns an appearance target into a number that can be compared across batches and styles.
nodes.ask: What SRM or EBC range does the beer need to land in?
nodes.range: About 1–40 SRM for common beers; EBC is roughly 2 × SRM

nodes.plain: The brewer adds oxygen to cooled wort before or at pitching so yeast can build healthy cell membranes.
nodes.does: Supports growth, shortens lag and helps yeast reach terminal gravity.
nodes.ask: How will I deliver about 8–10 ppm dissolved oxygen without contamination?
nodes.range: About 8–10 ppm; roughly 60 seconds of pure oxygen or 20 minutes of aeration as a practical proxy

items.name: Diacetyl
items.plain: Butter or popcorn. Cause: alpha-acetolactate and incomplete yeast cleanup, often exposed by an early crash or package.

items.name: Acetaldehyde
items.plain: Green apple or latex. Cause: young or incomplete fermentation, stressed yeast or infection.

items.name: DMS
items.plain: Cooked corn or cabbage. Cause: malt precursors, a weak or covered boil, or slow cooling.

items.name: Oxidation
items.plain: Papery, cardboard or stale hop notes. Cause: oxygen pickup after fermentation or during packaging.

items.name: Astringency
items.plain: Puckering, husky harshness. Cause: oversparging, over-crushing, or hot high-pH sparge water.

nodes.plain: Lagering time is the cold rest allowed after fermentation; stronger, rougher or hazier beers may need longer.
nodes.does: Gives yeast, proteins and polyphenols time to settle or transform.
nodes.ask: How many days or weeks will this beer need at its chosen cold temperature?
nodes.range: Roughly 2–8 weeks in traditional lagering schedules; choose by gravity, flavour and clarity

nodes.plain: The brewer raises temperature near terminal gravity so yeast can reduce diacetyl and its precursor.
nodes.does: Prevents buttery flavour from surviving into the package.
nodes.ask: When should I raise the beer by about 2–3°C, and is the forced test clean?
nodes.range: Raise about 2–3°C near terminal gravity; forced sample 60–71°C for 10–30 minutes

nodes.plain: Original gravity (OG) is the wort density before yeast; final gravity (FG) is the density after fermentation has finished.
nodes.does: Tracks extract, attenuation, ABV and whether a beer is ready to package.
nodes.ask: Are OG and FG on target, and is FG stable across repeated readings?
nodes.range: Common beer OG about 1.030–1.070; stable FG is more useful than a calendar date

assembly.title: Mash
assembly.text: Heat water, mix in crushed malt, hold the mash temperature and pH, then collect sweet wort.

assembly.title: Boil
assembly.text: Boil the wort, choose hop timing, drive off unwanted volatiles and set the bitterness target.

assembly.title: Ferment
assembly.text: Cool and oxygenate the boiled wort, pitch enough healthy yeast, and hold the fermentation profile until gravity settles.

assembly.title: Condition or lager
assembly.text: Let yeast clean up, run a diacetyl check, then choose the cold-conditioning temperature and time.

assembly.title: Package and serve
assembly.text: Clean and sanitise the package, transfer with minimal oxygen, carbonate at the chosen level, and pour the beer into the selected vessel.
